title: VIX spikes in history: 10 market panics and their causes

 A guide to VIX spikes in history and the market panics around them, from Black Monday in 1987 to the 2025 tariff selloff, and what caused each one
 1 / 12 List slides From Black Monday to the 2025 tariff selloff: 10 notable VIX spikes List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 5, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX index does not record what the stock market did. It records what traders expect the market to do over the next 30 days, as priced through options. That difference explains why its sharpest jumps tend to arrive when uncertainty is high and hard information is scarce. A volatility spike is a snapshot of investors paying up for protection before they know how bad things will get.
 Cboe introduced the VIX in 1993 as a measure of expected 30-day stock market volatility. In 2003 it rebuilt the calculation around S&P 500 options, the basis the index still uses. Cboe has also calculated the index back to 1990. Even that backfilled history leaves the first episode below, the October 1987 crash, outside the official data. It is included because it shows the kind of shock the gauge was later built to capture.
 The 10 episodes that follow, arranged in chronological order, are a selection of notable VIX spikes in history and the market panics behind them. They are not a ranking, and they are not a complete list. Some of them set records, including the highest intraday reading and the highest close the index has posted. Others stand out for the way they unfolded or for what they exposed about how markets are built.
 What links them is less the size of each move than the range of triggers behind it. A Russian debt default and a hedge fund collapse sit alongside a terror attack and the failure of a major investment bank. A downgrade of the U.S. government's credit rating, a currency devaluation in China and the collapse of products built to bet on calm also appear. The list closes with a pandemic, a shift in Japanese monetary policy and a sweeping round of U.S. tariffs.
 Each slide explains what happened, when it happened and how the Wall Street fear gauge responded. Closing and intraday levels appear only where reliable figures exist. For investors who follow stock market volatility, the episodes show that fear does not move on one schedule. Fear can build over weeks or arrive in a single session, and a spike can reverse within days. Comparing the triggers shows how differently a bank failure, a policy shift or a pandemic can move the index.
 Black Monday 1987 stock market crash before the VIX existed 
 Illustration: Quartz
 On Oct. 19, 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 22.6% in a single trading session. The VIX index did not exist yet. Cboe's published history for the gauge does not reach back to that day.
 The crash became known as Black Monday, after the day of the week on which the selloff hit.
 The missing reading matters for anyone comparing volatility spikes across decades. Any figure presented as the VIX level for October 1987 is not part of Cboe's record. That sets Black Monday apart from the later episodes in this list, which can be measured on the gauge itself.
 Black Monday still shows the type of event the index was later designed to track. A one-session collapse in the Dow of that size is the kind of sudden break in investor confidence that a gauge of expected stock market volatility was built to capture.
 Russian debt default and the LTCM collapse in 1998 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Russia defaulted on its domestic debt in August 1998, and the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management collapsed in the turmoil that followed. In September 1998, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York organized a private-sector rescue of the fund.
 The episode moved in three steps. A government stopped paying its own domestic obligations first. A single private investment firm failed next. A central bank responded last.
 The form of that response set the episode apart. The New York Fed did not take over Long-Term Capital Management. It brought private-sector firms together, and those firms carried out the rescue themselves.
 The shock began abroad, in a sovereign debt market. It reached Wall Street through the failure of one leveraged fund. That path ran from a foreign default to a U.S. hedge fund to a rescue brokered by the Fed. It shows how a problem in one country's debt market can reach U.S. markets through leverage.
 Sept. 11 attacks and the 2001 stock market reopening 
 Illustration: Quartz
 U.S. stock markets closed after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks and did not reopen until Sept. 17, 2001. When trading resumed, stock market volatility rose sharply as investors acted on the shock through U.S. exchanges for the first time.
 The episode unfolded in an unusual order. In most selloffs, prices and the VIX index react while the news is still coming in. In September 2001, the worst of the news arrived while U.S. exchanges were shut.
 The closure left uncertainty with no outlet on those exchanges. Investors holding U.S. stocks could not sell them there, and buyers could not step in. The session on Sept. 17 became the first chance to act on everything that had happened during the shutdown.
 The pause also affected the fear gauge itself. The VIX is built from option prices, and U.S. markets were closed. The index had no fresh trading to reflect the days right after the attacks. Its reading after the reopening captured the reaction to the whole period at once.
 That timing shaped the volatility spike. The sharp move after the reopening reflected an adjustment that had been held back. It did not build gradually across the days after the attacks.
 The trigger also sets this episode apart. Most of the other episodes in this list began inside the financial system or with a policy choice. The Sept. 11 attacks came from outside it entirely. No balance sheet, rate decision or trading strategy set off the move.
 For readers comparing spikes, the 2001 episode shows how a market closure can delay the response to a shock without removing it. Uncertainty that cannot be traded does not go away. It carries over to the next open session.
 VIX record intraday high of 89.53 in the 2008 financial crisis 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX hit 89.53 during trading on Oct. 24, 2008, the highest intraday reading in the index's history. The spike came weeks after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 15, 2008, as the global financial crisis spread through banks and credit markets.
 Lehman was a Wall Street investment bank with heavy exposure to U.S. real estate and mortgage-backed securities. Its filing remains the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history. Earlier in 2008, JPMorgan $JPM Chase bought Bear Stearns with Federal Reserve support. Lehman received no government rescue. Its collapse showed investors that a major Wall Street firm could be allowed to fail.
 The damage spread quickly. Merrill Lynch agreed to sell itself to Bank of America $BAC the same weekend Lehman collapsed. Within days, the Federal Reserve extended emergency credit to the insurer AIG. The Reserve Primary Fund, a money market fund that held Lehman debt, broke the buck. Its share value fell below the $1 level that such funds aim to hold.
 Banks grew wary of lending to one another, and short-term funding markets seized up. Stock investors could not tell which institutions were still solvent.
 Policymakers responded on several fronts. The House of Representatives voted down the first bank rescue bill on Sept. 29, 2008. A revised version, which created the Troubled Asset Relief Program, became law on Oct. 3. On Oct. 8, the Fed joined the European Central Bank, the Bank of England and other central banks in a coordinated interest rate cut. Neither step stopped the VIX from climbing to its peak later that month.
 The index did not jump once and fall back. It stayed at crisis levels through the autumn. On Nov. 20, 2008, it closed at 80.86, a record closing level at the time. The gap between the Oct. 24 intraday peak and the Nov. 20 closing record shows how long the stress lasted, not only how sharp it was at its worst.
 The 80.86 close held as the index's record until March 2020, when the COVID-19 selloff produced a higher close. The intraday mark has not been passed. That leaves 2008 as the episode that pushed the Wall Street fear gauge furthest within a single trading session.
 S&P downgrade of the U.S. credit rating in August 2011 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX closed at 48.00 on Aug. 8, 2011, the first trading day after Standard & Poor's cut the U.S. long-term credit rating from AAA to AA+. That close tied a spike in the Wall Street fear gauge directly to doubts about the creditworthiness of the world's largest economy.
 S&P announced the downgrade on Aug. 5, 2011. That was a Friday, and the decision came after U.S. markets had closed. Investors had the whole weekend to absorb the news. Their first chance to trade on it came when markets opened on Monday.
 It was the first time S&P had rated U.S. government debt below its top grade. Moody's $MCO and Fitch, the other two major rating agencies, kept their top ratings on the U.S. at the time. The move came from a single agency, not from the rating industry as a whole.
 The downgrade followed a long standoff in Washington over raising the federal debt ceiling. Congress and the White House reached a deal only shortly before the Treasury expected to run out of borrowing room. S&P pointed to the political process around that fight, not just the size of U.S. debt, as a factor in its decision.
 Europe added a second source of strain. The euro-zone debt crisis had already led to bailouts for Greece, Ireland and Portugal. By the summer of 2011, investors were also questioning the finances of larger economies such as Italy and Spain. Two of the world's major economic blocs were facing debt questions at the same time.
 The market reaction carried a contradiction. A downgrade of U.S. debt might be expected to push investors away from Treasuries. Instead, many buyers moved into U.S. government bonds as a haven while they sold stocks. The rating cut did not change the role Treasuries played in global markets during a period of stress.
 The 2011 spike differs from crises set off by a single failed firm or a sudden external shock. Its trigger was a judgment about sovereign credit risk, delivered by a private rating agency. That judgment landed on top of a political fight and a foreign debt crisis. For anyone tracking the VIX index, it is a case where stock market volatility jumped on policy and credit decisions. The financial system itself did not collapse.
 China yuan devaluation selloff of August 2015 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX jumped to an intraday high of 53.29 on Aug. 24, 2015, and closed at 40.74, up from a previous close of 28.03. The trigger was fear about China's economy, which had been building since Beijing devalued the yuan on Aug. 11, 2015.
 The People's Bank of China carried out the devaluation, and investors read it as a signal. A deliberate weakening of the currency suggested that Chinese policymakers were worried about growth. Markets had come to treat China as a dependable source of global demand, and that assumption suddenly looked shaky.
 The concern reached well beyond China's borders. China was a major buyer of commodities such as iron ore and copper. Many emerging economies counted it as a leading trading partner. Multinational companies relied on Chinese customers for a meaningful share of their sales. A slowdown in China threatened all of them at once, and that worry fed into stock market volatility in the U.S.
 The pressure came to a head on Monday, Aug. 24. The Shanghai Composite fell about 8.5% that day. The selling moved through Asian trading hours first and then reached Europe and New York as those markets opened.
 The VIX readings from that session show how far the fear gauge can travel within a single day. The intraday high came during the worst of the early confusion. The lower close reflected a market that had steadied somewhat later in the session. Even so, the index still finished well above where it had ended the previous trading day.
 The episode is also remembered for trouble in the market's plumbing. During parts of the day, many exchange-traded products traded at prices that broke away from the value of the assets they held. An investor who sold at the wrong moment could receive much less than the fund's underlying holdings were worth.
 Those dislocations drew attention to how exchange-traded funds behave under stress. They also raised questions about stop-loss orders, which become market orders once a trigger price is hit. In a disorderly open, such an order could fill far below the level the investor had in mind.
 The August 2015 spike differs from crises driven by failing banks or defaulting borrowers. No major U.S. institution collapsed. The shock began with a currency decision and a falling stock market in another country, and it still sent the Wall Street fear gauge sharply higher.
 Volmageddon and the collapse of the XIV short-volatility note in 2018 
 Illustration: Quartz
 On Feb. 5, 2018, the VIX rose 115.6% in a single session, closing at 37.32 after finishing the previous day at 17.31. That is the largest one-day percentage gain in the index's record, and the episode became known on Wall Street as "Volmageddon."
 Stocks fell hard that day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,175 points. The lasting damage, however, landed less on stocks than on a group of investment products built to profit from calm markets.
 Those products were short-volatility funds and notes. They were designed to gain when expected volatility stayed low or drifted lower. They lost money when it rose. For their holders, a quiet market produced steady returns. A sudden jump in the fear gauge did the opposite.
 The best-known casualty was Credit Suisse's VelocityShares Daily Inverse VIX Short-Term exchange-traded note, which traded under the ticker XIV. The note was built to deliver the inverse of the daily move in short-term VIX futures. Its exposure reset each day. That design meant one extreme session could wipe out gains built up over a long stretch of calm. Credit Suisse terminated the note soon after Feb. 5.
 An exchange-traded note differs from an exchange-traded fund in one structural way. It is an unsecured debt obligation of the bank that issues it, not a fund that holds underlying assets. The fate of XIV therefore rested on the terms Credit Suisse had written into the product.
 The 2018 spike also stands apart from other episodes in this selection. Its closing level of 37.32 sat well below the readings of the 2008 financial crisis or the 2020 pandemic crash. What defined the day was the speed of the move from a low starting point, not the height the index reached.
 For holders of short-volatility products, a single session undid the payoff from a long run of quiet markets. It also marked how quickly a bet on calm could unwind once the Wall Street fear gauge began to climb.
 COVID-19 crash and the record VIX close of 82.69 in March 2020 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX closed at 82.69 on March 16, 2020, the highest close in the index's history. The spread of COVID-19, widespread lockdowns and a rush to sell assets drove the reading, which passed the closing record set during the 2008 financial crisis.
 That earlier closing mark was 80.86, from Nov. 20, 2008. The 2008 crisis still holds the index's highest intraday reading, so the two episodes split the records between them. One owns the highest finish to a trading day, and the other owns the highest point reached during a session.
 The trigger in 2020 came from outside the financial system. In 2008, the stress started inside banks and spread outward into the wider economy. In 2020, a public health emergency halted ordinary economic activity first, and the financial strain followed.
 The World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic on March 11, 2020, the week before the record close. Governments moved quickly to contain the virus. Lockdowns closed offices, stores, restaurants and much of global travel within a short span. Investors were left unsure about revenue across nearly every industry at once.
 The result was a broad rush to sell. Investors moved out of stocks and other assets in search of cash. Selling on March 16 was heavy enough to trigger a market-wide circuit breaker shortly after the opening bell, halting trading on U.S. exchanges. It was one of several such halts that month.
 The Federal Reserve acted the day before the record close. On March 15, 2020, a Sunday, the central bank cut its policy rate to near zero. The decision came outside its regular meeting schedule. The Fed also announced it would resume large-scale purchases of Treasury and mortgage-backed securities.
 The record close arrived on the very next trading day. Neither the rate cut nor the bond-buying plan stopped the index from reaching its highest close. Traders were still paying heavily for protection against further losses in stocks.
 Yen carry trade unwind and the August 2024 VIX spike 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The VIX closed at 38.57 on Aug. 5, 2024, after trading intraday near 65.73, its highest reading of the episode. The spike followed a Bank of Japan rate increase and a weak U.S. jobs report, which together set off a rapid unwind of yen-funded carry trades.
 A carry trade starts with borrowing in a currency that carries a low interest rate. The borrowed money then goes into assets that pay more, such as higher-yielding bonds or stocks in other markets. The profit comes from the gap between the cost of the loan and the return on the investment. For years, Japan's interest rates sat near or below zero. That made the yen a common funding currency for these positions.
 The strategy holds up only while the funding currency stays cheap and stable. If the borrowed currency strengthens, the loan becomes more expensive to repay. If interest rates in the funding country rise, the cost of holding the position rises too. Either change can push investors to sell what they bought and repay what they borrowed.
 The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate on July 31, 2024. The increase lifted the cost of borrowing in yen. On Aug. 2, a weak U.S. jobs report raised concern that the American economy was slowing. Soft labor data can lead investors to expect lower U.S. interest rates. Lower U.S. rates would shrink the gap that made yen-funded trades attractive.
 The two pressures arrived in the same week. Investors who had borrowed in yen faced higher funding costs and thinner expected returns at the same time. Many of them sold positions to cut their exposure, and the unwind added to selling in stock markets.
 The Wall Street fear gauge hit its peak for the episode on Monday, Aug. 5. Most of that jump did not hold. The intraday reading near 65.73 sat far above the close at 38.57, which means much of the surge faded before the session ended. The early move showed how much traders were willing to pay for protection in the first hours of trading, before the selling had run its course.
 The index fell back quickly in the days that followed. That fast retreat separates the 2024 spike from episodes in which fear stayed elevated for weeks. The event showed how leverage built on a single funding currency can carry a policy change in Tokyo into U.S. stock market volatility within days.
 U.S. tariff announcement selloff of April 2025 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The sweeping U.S. tariff announcement of April 2, 2025 set off a stock market selloff that pushed the VIX above 60 during trading on April 7, 2025. A day later, on April 8, the Wall Street fear gauge closed above 50.
 The trigger in this case was a change in U.S. trade policy. No institution failed, and no borrower missed a payment. The shock came from a government decision about the terms on which goods would cross U.S. borders.
 Trade policy reaches stock prices through several channels. Tariffs can change import costs for companies that buy from abroad. They can disrupt supply chains that run through several countries. They can also alter the outlook for the economies of trading partners. A single sweeping announcement can raise questions on all of those fronts in the same moment.
 The timing of the readings shows how the fear built. The announcement came on a Wednesday. The index did not cross 60 until trading on the following Monday, April 7. That gap means this volatility spike was not a one-session reaction to a headline. Expectations of turbulence kept climbing as investors weighed what the policy would mean.
 The two April readings also measure different things. The figure above 60 captures how high expected volatility was priced at points during the April 7 session. The close above 50 captures where that expectation stood when trading ended on April 8. A close at that level, a day after the intraday peak, means the pressure had not faded by the next final bell.
 For scale, the April 2025 readings stayed below the index's records. The highest intraday reading is 89.53, set on Oct. 24, 2008. The highest close is 82.69, reached on March 16, 2020.
 The April 8 close still sat above the closing levels of two earlier episodes. The VIX closed at 48.00 on Aug. 8, 2011, after the U.S. credit downgrade. It closed at 40.74 on Aug. 24, 2015, after China's yuan devaluation.
